title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
summary: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution covers persistence achieved by configuring code to run automatically when a system starts, when a user logs on, or when a session state changes. Rather than one mechanism, the parent technique collects the many autostart surfaces an operating system offers: registry keys and startup folders on Windows, launch agents, launch daemons and login items on macOS, init scripts, systemd units, cron entries and shell profiles on Linux, plus vendor extension points such as print monitors, authentication packages, security support providers and browser helper components. Adversaries favour these locations because they are legitimate features, they execute early or in a privileged context, and they are frequently ignored by users and asset owners alike. The evidence is largely static and configuration-based: registry values pointing at unusual binaries, new or modified service and unit definitions, changes to shell startup files, scheduled tasks with logon triggers, and file creation in autostart directories. Because thousands of such entries are legitimately present on any mature endpoint, the useful question is not whether autostart entries exist but whether one changed recently, points to an unsigned or user-writable location, runs with higher privilege than the account that created it, or coincides with other incident activity on the same host. Baselines built from known-good images, combined with change tracking on autostart locations and file integrity monitoring, reduce an unmanageable list to a small set of reviewable differences. That same baseline supports recovery, because persistence removal during containment has to be complete without breaking the legitimate startup software an organisation depends on.
objectives: Enumerate the principal autostart locations on Windows, Linux and macOS and the privilege each confers on the executed code.
Use baselining and change tracking to reduce autostart review to a manageable set of differences.
Interpret endpoint telemetry for processes launched at boot, logon or session state change.
Judge suspicious autostart entries by path writability, signature state, parent privilege and recency.
Plan persistence removal during containment without breaking legitimate startup software.
Write detection logic for new autostart entries that reference user-writable or unsigned binaries.
